title: The vowels
hook: hey and heyyyy are different messages; Pali writes the stretch into the word
tomorrow: why does dhamma have an h that's so hard to hear?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pali: the Buddha let his words go out in every dialect, and the chants came to rest in this one. The words behind the chants. And behind that, a run of endings and openings: all things end, a fresh year, the heart of it, look how far, many doors.
screen: `THE WORDS BEHIND THE CHANTS.` → `ENDINGS AND OPENINGS.`

segments.voice: In a text, hey and heyyyy are not the same message. Nobody taught you that rule. You just know a stretched sound is carrying something a short one isn't. Pali writes the stretch into the spelling. Some vowels are short, clipped. Some are long, held. That's why a chant leans on some sounds and hurries past others. It isn't a temple's style. It's the words themselves.
screen: `HEY IS NOT HEYYYY.` → `PALI SPELLS THE STRETCH.` → `NOT STYLE: THE WORDS THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Here they are. Three short ones: a, said like the u in but; i, like the i in pin; u, like the u in put. Three long ones, the same sounds held: a, like father; i, like machine; u, like rule. In roman letters, the long ones wear a little bar on top. Then e, as in they, and o, as in go, which count as long, with one catch: before a double consonant they go short, as in metta. Teachers say a long vowel takes about twice the time of a short one. Yesterday's word shows it: Pali is a long a, then a short i. Dhamma is two short a's, quick and open. Nibbana goes short, long, short. Get the lengths right and a chant keeps its shape, because the old verses are built on a pattern of long and short. Stretch everything and the pattern smears. Clip everything and it rushes. Open vowels, each given its own time.
screen: `SHORT: A, I, U.` · `LONG: THE SAME SOUNDS, HELD.` · `E AND O: LONG, WITH A CATCH.` · `NIBBANA: SHORT, LONG, SHORT.` · then, large: `OPEN VOWELS.`

segments.voice: Say each vowel slowly, out loud, one to a breath: a, then aa; i, then ee; u, then oo; then e, and o. Let the short ones stay short and give the long ones their full time, then rest in the quiet after the last o.
The vowels. Short a, i and u; long a, i and u; and e and o. The open floor every chant stands on.
Hold on to this: open vowels, where short stays short and long gets its time. Two days into Pali.

howItsDone: Theravada chanting books often print the Pali in roman letters with marks over the long vowels, and new chanters learn the lengths by ear, chanting along with monks and longtime lay chanters.

pairs: the long a, as in father
the short a, like the u in but
the long i, as in machine
an e gone short before a double t

myth: in a chant, every vowel is stretched slow and even
short ones stay short and long ones are held; that pattern is the chant's rhythm.
a bar over a letter, as in ā, marks a long vowel
in roman letters, ā, ī and ū are the long ones, held about twice as long, teachers say.
e and o are long in every Pali word
they count as long, but go short before a double consonant, as in metta.

fork.setup: your chant sheet has no bars over any letters, and you reach the word nibbana. which a do you hold?
options: the middle one: nibbana goes short, long, short, marked or not.
all three: long vowels are what make a chant sound right.
none: the bars are decoration for scholars, so clip them all.
fork.reveal: the bar only shows the length; the length belongs to the word. nibbana holds its middle a, whether the sheet marks it or not.

original.note: the Pali vowels in Devanagari letters: short a, long ā, short i, long ī, short u, long ū, then e and o.

trapdoor: what you thought: chanting means stretching every sound slow and even.
what it means: Pali spells length into the word: short a, i and u, long ā, ī and ū, and e and o counted long.
what a scholar hears: the old verses are built on a pattern of long and short syllables, so vowel length is the chant's rhythm, not a temple's style.
guess: the open sounds a chant is built on, short and long
the silent letters chanters skip when going fast
the high notes a lead chanter sings on their own

chat.says: practiced the temple chant sheet at dinner. ông laughed at my "naaaamo." am i stretching it wrong?
options: A little. In namo the a is short and the o is long, so hold only the o.
Not really. Stretch every vowel the same; slow and even is what makes a chant.
It doesn't matter. Vowel length is just a style each temple picks for itself.
chat.meaning: Pali writes length into the word: a, i and u come short or long, and e and o count as long. Only the long ones are held.

metta.meaning: loving-kindness; its e goes short before the double t

notes: Pronunciation guide (short a as the u in but; i as in pin; u as in put; long ā as in father; ī as in machine; ū as in rule; e as in they; o as in go) follows common Pali grammars (e.g. Duroiselle 1906); confirm the English sound-alikes are the ones a Theravada teacher would use.
'e and o count as long, but go short before a double consonant (metta)': standard grammar rule, paraphrased; confirm.
'Teachers say a long vowel takes about twice the time of a short one' (one vs two matta) is hedged as teachers' guidance; confirm.
'The old verses are built on a pattern of long and short' refers to quantitative Pali meter; stated generally on purpose. Confirm wording.

The outline's hook groups e and o with the long vowels; the script keeps that and adds the short-before-double-consonant catch. If the Keeper prefers the outline's simpler version for an elective, the metta line can be cut.
nibbana gloss meaning ('the going-out of greed, hatred and delusion') follows the Samyutta's definition (SN 38.1) as taught in earlier years; confirm.
Review shape: games.recall holds the six most recent carries (days 1422–1427) for the review round; the review segment names them briefly. A light vowel teach is kept, as the outline requires.
